quiz.q: What are the three kinds of procedural macros?
options: Derive, attribute, and function-like
Struct, enum, and trait
Sync, async, and blocking
Public, private, and crate-level
quiz.explain: Proc macros come in three flavors: derive (#[derive(X)]), attribute (#[tokio::main]), and function-like (sqlx::query!(...)).

quiz.q: What does `#[derive(Serialize)]` actually do to your struct's own definition?
options: Rewrites the struct's fields
Nothing to the definition itself — it generates a separate impl Serialize block next to it
Deletes any unused fields
Converts the struct into an enum
quiz.explain: A derive macro adds new code (typically a trait impl) alongside your type. Your original struct or enum definition is never touched.

quiz.q: Why can't `fn main()` directly contain top-level `async` code without help?
options: Async functions can't return values
Something has to create an async runtime and drive the future — that's what an attribute macro like #[tokio::main] generates for you
main() can never be async in any language
It actually can, no macro is needed
quiz.explain: #[tokio::main] rewrites your async fn main into a plain fn main that builds a Tokio runtime and blocks on your async body — Rust has no built-in async main.

quiz.q: What makes `sqlx::query!("...")` different from an ordinary macro_rules! macro, even though both are called as name!(...)?
options: Nothing — they work identically
sqlx::query! is a function-like proc macro that can do real compile-time work, like checking your SQL against a live database schema
macro_rules! macros are always faster to compile
sqlx::query! can only be used inside tests
quiz.explain: Function-like proc macros look like macro_rules! calls but are full Rust programs that can inspect external state (a DB schema, a file) at compile time — something pure token-matching can never do.

quiz.q: What must a crate that defines a proc macro set in its Cargo.toml?
options: edition = "2021"
`proc-macro = true` under [lib]
`crate-type = ["cdylib"]`
Nothing special is required
quiz.explain: Proc macro crates declare `proc-macro = true` under [lib] — which also means they can only export macros, not ordinary structs or functions.

quiz.q: Why can't you define a proc macro and use it in the same crate?
options: It's only a stylistic convention, not enforced
A proc macro must be compiled as its own artifact before the compiler can run it while compiling other code
Proc macros can only be written in a different language
Cargo doesn't allow more than one macro per crate
quiz.explain: The compiler runs proc macro code as part of compiling other crates, so the macro crate has to already be built and available — it can't be defined and consumed in a single compilation pass.

options: Adds new dependencies to Cargo.toml automatically
Shows the fully macro-expanded source code, so you can see exactly what a derive or attribute macro generated
Increases your binary size for release builds
Converts macro_rules! macros into proc macros
quiz.explain: cargo expand runs your crate through real macro expansion and pretty-prints the result — the fastest way to understand or debug generated code.

quiz.q: This fails to compile: `use serde::Serialize; struct User { id: u64 } fn main() { serde_json::to_string(&User { id: 1 }).unwrap(); }`. What's missing?
options: A semicolon after the struct definition
`#[derive(Serialize)]` above the struct — importing the trait doesn't implement it
serde_json needs to be imported separately
User needs a Debug impl
quiz.explain: `use serde::Serialize;` only brings the trait name into scope; it doesn't implement it for User. Only `#[derive(Serialize)]` actually generates that implementation.

flashcards.front: Name the three kinds of procedural macros.
flashcards.back: Derive macros (#[derive(X)]), attribute macros (#[tokio::main]), and function-like macros (sqlx::query!(...)).

flashcards.front: Does a derive macro modify your struct or enum's own definition?
flashcards.back: No — it generates separate code (usually a trait impl) alongside your type. The definition you wrote stays exactly as-is.

flashcards.front: What does #[tokio::main] actually do to an `async fn main`?
flashcards.back: It replaces it with a plain fn main() that builds a Tokio runtime and blocks on your async body — Rust has no native async main.

flashcards.front: What makes sqlx::query! different from a macro_rules! macro that looks the same at the call site?
flashcards.back: It's a proc macro that can do real compile-time work — like connecting to a database to check your SQL and column types — something pattern-matching macros can't do.

flashcards.front: What Cargo.toml setting marks a crate as a proc macro crate?
flashcards.back: `proc-macro = true` under [lib]. Such a crate can only export macros, not ordinary items.

flashcards.front: Why must a proc macro live in a different crate than the one that uses it?
flashcards.back: The compiler runs the macro's code while compiling other crates, so the macro crate must already be built as its own artifact first — it can't be defined and used in the same compilation.

flashcards.front: What's the fastest way to see what a derive macro actually generated?
flashcards.back: Run `cargo expand` — it prints the fully expanded, real Rust source.

flashcards.front: A struct imports `serde::Serialize` but fails `serde_json::to_string` with a 'trait bound not satisfied' error. What's the fix?
flashcards.back: Add `#[derive(Serialize)]` above the struct. Importing the trait only lets you refer to it; deriving it is what actually implements it.
